content: To ensure a comprehensive and transparent process in the development of guidelines, it is recommended to consider publishing an open call for nominees when forming technical networks, collaborating centers, and formally appointed expert advisory panels. Established guideline development groups within the World Health Organization (WHO) already have nomination procedures in place that can serve as a reference. Regardless of the methods used to select members, the decision-making process must be thoroughly documented. This documentation should include the following key elements: Relevant technical expertise. Individuals responsible for implementing the guidelines, such as program managers and healthcare professionals. Representatives of groups most affected by the guidelines, such as patients. Methodologists with expertise in evidence assessment, guideline development, health economics, and statistics, as needed. The group must appoint a writer for the guideline. This individual should be involved throughout all planning and development stages to ensure the guideline is clearly written and the process is well-documented. This is critical for final clearance and subsequent implementation. Including end-users, either as part of the guideline development group or in an external review group, increases the likelihood of producing a guideline that meets their needs and is effectively implemented. The selection of the chair for the group is a pivotal decision. The chair should be skilled in facilitating group discussions and interpreting evidence. While content knowledge is important, individuals with strong biases regarding specific interventions should not chair the group. If a content expert is chosen as chair, measures to reduce bias, such as ensuring the chair does not have veto power, should be implemented. Technical content experts are selected based on their expertise in the subject matter of the guideline. A balanced group should include a range of expertise and affiliations, with representatives from professional groups responsible for implementing the guideline in various regions. For example, palliative care nurses may be included for guidelines on pain management. Although finding such representatives for global guidelines can be challenging, international consumer groups and non-governmental organizations in many countries can provide members who may participate as observers or full members. Involving consumers in guideline groups ensures that: The questions addressed are relevant to consumers. Relevant aspects of the experience of illness are considered. Critical outcomes are identified and prioritized. The final guideline is understandable to those it affects. Barriers to consumer participation include the lack of suitable consumer groups, time constraints, and the complexity of scientific terminology used by committees. However, experience from organizations like the United Kingdom’s National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence demonstrates that consumers, when provided with training and support, make critical contributions to guideline development. Many WHO guideline groups include a methodologist, an expert in guideline development processes, to complement the technical expertise of subject-matter experts. Methodologists should be consulted during the planning stage, before the guideline development group is formed, as they can provide valuable advice on group composition. An economist should be included to advise on the potential economic benefits and drawbacks of the recommendations being considered. The economist should also guide the group on how to search for evidence on resource use and costs associated with likely recommendations and interpret that evidence. It is strongly recommended that one person be designated as the writer/editor for the guideline. This individual will be responsible for drafting the guideline, with the rest of the group reviewing and endorsing the document. When external review comments are received, the same person should finalize the document to ensure coherence, clarity, and accuracy. During meetings, the chair should ensure that all members can present their views, that assumptions are debated, and that discussions are open and constructive. The chair must keep the group focused on the agenda and the project timeline. Conflicts of interest must be managed and reported. Declarations of interest should be collected and reviewed before appointments are made, and any changes must be reported to the secretariat. At the meeting, participants should verbally report potential conflicts of interest, and any changes to declarations should be recorded in the meeting minutes. The guideline development group meeting must cover a significant amount of material in a short time. To ensure effectiveness, all participants should understand their roles and expected outputs. Clear information should be provided about the scope, roles, tasks, and processes of the meeting. If the purpose of the meeting is to sign off on questions for guideline development, a draft set of questions should be prepared and circulated to participants in advance. If the purpose is to formulate recommendations, evidence profiles should be distributed at least a week prior to the meeting, and draft recommendations prepared by the WHO steering group should be presented for review and revision. Conflicts of interest occur when professional judgment regarding a primary interest, such as patient welfare or research validity, is unduly influenced by a secondary interest, such as financial gain. Declaring a secondary interest does not automatically preclude participation in a guideline development group or expert review group. However, WHO defines a conflict of interest as any interest held by an expert that may affect or reasonably be perceived to affect their objectivity and independence in providing advice. The WHO process for managing interests includes: 1. Experts and advisors complete Declaration of Interest (DOI) forms before the guideline meeting. 2. The WHO steering group assesses declared interests to determine whether a conflict exists that may preclude or limit participation. 3. At each meeting, DOI forms are summarized and presented to the group, allowing members to update or amend their declarations. Management strategies for each member are also presented. 4. All declared interests are reported in the final guideline document. Financial, academic, and public position interests must be declared. Financial conflicts include personal financial gain, grants, shares, or employment related to the guideline topic. Academic conflicts and public positions may also affect objectivity and independence. Decisions on managing declared interests are made on a case-by-case basis. Participants with significant personal financial interests in a single company with a commercial interest in the guideline outcome should not participate. Participants with links to multiple companies or those who have received research funding from relevant companies may participate in discussions but should be recused during the development of recommendations. All decisions on managing declared interests must be documented before the meeting and included in the final guideline. Legal counsel will provide advice on handling individual cases.
